cards.headline: Mountains beyond mountains
cards.snippet: The subtitle comes from Tracy Kidder's 2003 book Mountains Beyond Mountains, about Dr. Paul Farmer's work in Haiti — its title a Haitian Kreyòl proverb for obstacles that never end. Régine Chassagne sings lead on the album's synth-pop outlier, trading the band's orchestral swell for a sequencer pulse as she plays a singer ordered back to her day job.
cards.context: Win Butler cited Kidder's book as the song's primary inspiration in Vanity Fair, August 2010.

cards.headline: The video that danced back
cards.snippet: Vincent Morisset directed two videos, both released December 13, 2011: a traditional one following Chassagne through a paper-mâché suburb, and an interactive twin in which the viewer dances in front of a webcam to speed the song up — stand still and it slows to a dirge. The song closed the decade on Pitchfork's and NME's best-of-the-2010s lists.
cards.context: Pitchfork named it Best New Track on release; it ranks #50 (Pitchfork) and #20 (NME) for the 2010s.

cards.headline: Told to punch the clock
cards.snippet: The song opens with its singer ordered off the stage of her own life: singing is treated as a disturbance, and the day job's clock is the cure. Genius annotators hear 'pretentious' as a jab returned — the word critics kept hanging on Arcade Fire themselves.
cards.context: It is the line listeners quote back most; one calls 'punch the clock' the most triggering lyric they know.

cards.headline: The angel song, found after three years
cards.snippet: ive been looking for this song for 3 years, its my dads favorite song and he used to play it for me when i was a kid and we would dance around the living room. he passed away in 2018 and all ive been doing is looking for this song and i just remembered me calling it the angel song because he told mne the women singing were angels. i looked up arcade fire angel song so many times i cant count. then i remembered seeing something about mountains. i found it now and i can finally just listen to it.
cards.context: The official video's top comment: a three-year search for 'the angel song' she danced to with her father, found again from one remembered word — mountains.

cards.headline: Nostalgic on the second listen
cards.snippet: How does every single Arcade Fire song manage to make you feel so nostalgic? This is only my second time hearing this song and I feel like I've known this band forever. I love coming across bands like this so much <3
cards.context: Nostalgia on a second listen — the replies credit the '80s voices the song channels.

cards.headline: She dances as if no one's watching
cards.snippet: I love everything about Regine, from her child-like mannerisms, to the way she dances as if no ones watching. She's such an inspiration to me.
cards.context: On the official video, where Chassagne dances through a paper suburb in a sequined dress.

cards.headline: Soulwax takes it to the disco
cards.snippet: Soulwax's remix, previewed on BBC Radio 1 in March 2012 and released that April, stretches the song past six minutes of filter-disco; it has 1.1 million views on Soulwax's channel. One listener: "Arcade Fire + Soulwax = The Knife"

cards.headline: Two voices in an empty room
cards.snippet: In the summer of 2020 Win Butler and Régine Chassagne performed the song as a duo in New Orleans, her voice over keyboards in an empty room; the video, posted that September, has 1.1 million views. One listener: "Neighbours: 'People next door are doing Arcade Fire Karaoke.'"

cards.headline: Closes the Stuart Fails finale
cards.snippet: The Big Bang Theory spinoff ends its first season (September 24, 2026) with its characters walking off the studio lot into the dark as this song begins — the finale's closing music, and the cue reviewers singled out. Its effect is still visible: the official video's newest comments are full of viewers the finale sent there.
cards.context: Processed Media called the ending 'incredibly poignant'; HBO Max renewed the show for a second season.
